description: Quạt máy: a pedestal fan with a blue plastic grille and a timer knob that ticks.  Every room in Saigon has one turned towards the bed.  Plug it in or hook it to a battery to stir the air.
Đèn dầu: a glass-chimney kerosene lamp kept under the stairs for the power cuts.
A thick red candle printed with gold characters, burnt on the family altar for the anniversaries of the dead.
A chunky 2G mobile phone with a monochrome screen, a snake game and a battery that lasts a week.  The network is dead, but it still tells the time and works as a torch.

A silver radio-cassette player with twin speakers and a carrying handle, still holding a tape of cải lương opera.  Use it to tune in whatever is still on the air, or to play the tape.  Each use drains a little of the battery.

description: Mùng: a white nylon net that hangs from four strings over a bed.  Without it the canal mosquitoes would eat you alive, and with the fever about nobody sleeps without one.

A tiny bottle of green medicated oil smelling of menthol and eucalyptus.  Rubbed on temples, belly or a stuffy nose it eases headaches, nausea and the misery of the heat.  Every grandmother carries one.
A foil sachet of oral rehydration salts.  Dissolved in a litre of clean water it replaces what diarrhoea and the heat take out of you.
Khẩu trang: a washable cotton mask in a flowery print with ear loops, worn by every motorbike rider against the dust and the sun.  It does little against the fever.
